explains: A token is a thing that CARRIES STATE — a number or a marker that a case holds, spends, loses and sometimes gets back. Places say where a case is; tokens say what it is holding while it is there. The single most important column below is `stored`: inside a battle, tokens are real mutable state living in memory for the length of the fight, and every one of them is thrown away at the end. In the court, almost nothing is stored at all — the numbers are READINGS, recomputed from the records every time anybody asks, which is why a grudge can be answered and a betrayal can be foreseen.

fields.name: What to call it in plain words.
fields.heldBy: What holds it — a unit, a contingent, an army, a house, the crown.
fields.flow: The machine this token most belongs to (data/flows.json), where one owns it.
fields.range: The values it runs between, and in what units. Battle bars run 0..1,000,000 inside the machine and are shown divided down; court scores run 0..100.
fields.stored: TRUE if it is real mutable state that is written and read back. FALSE if it is a READING — computed fresh from the records every time, never stored anywhere. This one field explains most of the difference between how the battle works and how the court works.
fields.refills: What, if anything, restores it — and `never` is a real and common answer.
fields.cites: The constant paths that govern it, dotted, exactly as in data/constants.json.
fields.explains: What holding this token feels like, and what running out of it does to you.

tokens.name: Nerve
tokens.range: 0 to 1,000,000 in the machine; shown as 0-100
tokens.gainedBy: winning, killing, a captain exhorting, steady friends nearby, the Tide running your way
tokens.spentBy: casualties, being shot at, friends breaking nearby, losing the banner, being flanked
tokens.refills: slowly, while out of contact — and never above the unit's ceiling
tokens.explains: The bar the whole game is about. What makes it interesting is the CEILING: a unit's nerve can never rise above a limit set before the battle by the court — by how much the men believe in the cause, how well they were fed, how far they marched. You do not fix a low ceiling on the field. You fixed it, or failed to, months ago.

tokens.name: The Ceiling on Nerve
tokens.gainedBy: resolve brought from the court — loyalty, a legitimate cause, veterancy, defending their own homes
tokens.spentBy: hunger, and erosion from sustained exhaustion during the battle itself
tokens.refills: never, within a battle — it only ever falls
tokens.explains: The most important number a player never looks at. It is the bridge from the court to the battlefield: everything you did politically arrives here, as a hard cap on how brave these men are capable of being today. Hungry men who marched a long way for a cause they do not believe in have a low ceiling, and no amount of brilliant handling will make them fight like a household guard.

tokens.name: The Floor Under Nerve
tokens.gainedBy: being paid — professionals have a floor beneath which they do not sink
tokens.spentBy: arrears; an unpaid mercenary loses his floor entirely
tokens.explains: The counterpart to the ceiling and the sharpest lesson about hiring soldiers. A paid professional will not break below a certain point no matter how bad it gets — that steadiness is exactly what you bought. Miss a season's wages and the floor goes away, which means the men you hired precisely because they would hold are now the men most likely to leave.

tokens.name: Cohesion
tokens.range: 0 to 1,000,000 in the machine; shown as 0-100
tokens.spentBy: moving fast, turning, rough ground, taking a charge, and breaking (which throws all of it away at once)
tokens.refills: by standing still — the most underrated order in the game
tokens.explains: How neat the formation is, and it multiplies everything that depends on the line being a line — refusal against cavalry above all. A ragged spear line braces badly and gets ridden over. This is why running your spearmen into position and bracing them the same second does not save them: they arrive with the cohesion spent.

tokens.name: Fatigue
tokens.range: 0 to 1,000,000; starts at whatever the march left in their legs
tokens.gainedBy: everything — standing costs a little, walking more, fighting more, charging most
tokens.refills: never within a battle; between battles, by resting
tokens.explains: A one-way tap that never turns off. Fatigue slows men down, makes them miss, and eventually starts eating the ceiling on their nerve — and crucially, they ARRIVE with some, put there by the roads and the season. Heavily armoured men tire faster, which is the price of everything that makes them good, and it is why a knight who has been fighting for an hour is a different animal from one who has not.

tokens.name: Arrows
tokens.spentBy: every volley — and aimed volleys cost a multiple
tokens.explains: Finite, and the finiteness is the whole design. Archers who spend the battle shooting at whatever is nearest will be empty when the thing that actually matters arrives. Aimed volleys hit far harder and cost several times the arrows, which makes every shooting decision a question about what you are saving them for.

tokens.name: Men Standing
tokens.spentBy: being killed, and being captured — which come out of the same tally
tokens.explains: How many are left. Note that captured men leave the tally exactly like dead ones — from inside the battle they are equally gone — and only the aftermath sorts out which is which. That sorting is where a good physician earns his stipend, because a wounded man who lives is a man you have next season.

tokens.name: The Second Chance
tokens.explains: The smallest token in the game and one of the most decisive. Every unit may come back from a rout exactly once. A commander who knows which of his units have spent theirs is playing a different game from one who does not — because a rallied unit looks like a unit and has nothing behind it.

tokens.name: Orders You Can Have Out
tokens.range: two to six, set by the Marshal's seat
tokens.gainedBy: filling the Marshalcy with a good man who likes you
tokens.spentBy: issuing an order; returned when it resolves
tokens.explains: The court's most direct hand on the battle's controls, and the clearest single argument for caring about the council table. A vacant Marshalcy means you fight the entire war two contingents at a time; a great Marshal gives you six. It is the same battle, the same army and the same enemy — and one of them you can actually conduct.

tokens.name: Blood Up
tokens.range: rises through the pursuit to a cap
tokens.explains: The reason won battles get thrown away. The longer a unit chases, the less interested it becomes in being called back — and since the command phase does not even run during a pursuit, you cannot call it back anyway. Cavalry that vanishes over the hill after a broken wing is the oldest mistake in warfare and this token is it.

tokens.name: The Tide
tokens.gainedBy: recent good news — kills, ground taken, enemies breaking
tokens.spentBy: recent bad news, and by time, as everything decays out of the window
tokens.refills: continuously — it is a reading over a moving window, not a score
tokens.explains: How the day FEELS, to men who cannot see the whole field. It is never stored anywhere: it is computed fresh from the recent event log, with older events counting for less, which means it recovers on its own if the bleeding stops. It is also the second condition on treachery — a wavering vassal turns when the Tide is against you, and not before.

tokens.name: Days in the Cup
tokens.range: 0 to whatever the enfeoffment record set
tokens.spentBy: every day that house's men stand in your army
tokens.refills: once a year, in full, used or not
tokens.explains: The game's title made into arithmetic. Each house is a cup holding one year of service, and the size of the cup was written into the grant when you enfeoffed them — the grant IS the contract. Because it refills whether you used it or not, unspent service is service lost, which quietly rewards a king who fights on a schedule over one who fights on impulse.

tokens.name: The Weight of a Grudge
tokens.range: 0 to 100, per grievance, and they add up
tokens.gainedBy: things you did, on dates, that are on the record
tokens.refills: not applicable — but a new wrong is a new grievance, not a bigger old one
tokens.explains: Never stored — always computed from the acts behind it, which is the single most important design choice in the court. Because it is a reading, making amends genuinely works: you add a record, and every future reading sees both. And because grievances add rather than merge, eleven small ones are a serious problem with no single cause to point at.

tokens.name: Standing
tokens.gainedBy: victories, justice done in public, ransoms paid for your own men, wars that were obviously right
tokens.spentBy: defeats, broken promises, abandoned captives, an idle summer after a victory
tokens.refills: not applicable — it is read fresh, every time
tokens.explains: What the realm thinks of you, and it reaches everywhere — into how much a captive of yours is worth, into whether a captain heeds an order, into whether a house sends men or excuses. Like everything else in the court it is a reading, so there is no hoarding it and no hiding a bad year: it is exactly what the record says about you, recomputed on demand.

tokens.name: Crowns
tokens.range: as much as the coffer holds
tokens.spentBy: wages, mercenary contracts, provisions, stipends, ransoms paid, amends
tokens.explains: Read from the record of every payment and receipt, never held as a balance. Coin is the one token that converts into almost every other: it buys men who owe you nothing, food that stops hunger eating your morale ceiling, amends that cool a grudge, and the freedom of your own captured vassals. Running out of it is rarely what kills you — what kills you is what you stopped paying for.

tokens.name: Grain
tokens.range: as many sacks as the granary holds
tokens.gainedBy: provisioning before you march, and foraging off the country
tokens.spentBy: every hundred men, every day, without exception
tokens.refills: by season — abundantly at harvest, barely at all in winter
tokens.explains: The clock on every campaign. Men who go without food gain hunger, hunger lowers the ceiling on their nerve, and a low ceiling loses battles before they start. Winter is dangerous not because of the cold but because forage nearly stops, so the granary drains at full rate against nothing coming in — which is how an army is destroyed without ever meeting an enemy.

tokens.name: Back Pay
tokens.explains: The most direct line in the game between a decision at court and a disaster on the field. Every unpaid season adds to a contingent's treachery AND removes the morale floor that made professionals worth hiring. Men you engaged precisely because they would stand are now both the likeliest to break and the likeliest to turn — and you can read the exact number beforehand.

tokens.name: Experience
tokens.heldBy: a unit, across its whole life
tokens.gainedBy: time spent in real contact — not battles attended, contact
tokens.spentBy: nothing; but it dies with the men who hold it
tokens.explains: Earned by minutes of actual fighting rather than by showing up, and capped per battle so a single bloodbath does not mint an elite. It feeds resolve, which feeds the ceiling on nerve — meaning a unit that has survived three hard fights is genuinely braver than an identical one that has not. It is also the strongest argument against spending men freely: veterancy is the one thing in this game that cannot be bought, only kept alive.
